editorNote: IBM cuts PC-family prices while Washington retreats from E-COM and home-computer owners debate smarter games, software prices and copy protection.
morningLine: Monday, June 4, 1984: the personal-computer market braces for lower IBM prices and a livelier summer software season.

lead.headline: IBM Cuts Prices Across the PC Line
lead.dek: Lower tags on personal computers, drives, displays and adapters turn up the pressure in an increasingly crowded compatible market.
body: IBM moved to sharpen its position in personal computing this week with price reductions across portions of the PC line. The changes reached beyond a single box: the company’s June hardware list covered the PC, XT, Portable PC, disk drives, displays and adapters, giving dealers and buyers a fresh schedule for assembling complete systems.

The cuts matter because IBM’s list prices set a powerful reference point for the entire market. Compatible makers have been selling on lower cost, added memory or bundled storage; a cheaper genuine IBM system narrows their room and forces every showroom comparison to be recalculated.

For business buyers, the headline price is only the beginning. A useful desk system still needs a monitor, storage, printer or communications hardware and software. Reductions among those supporting parts can change a purchase order as much as a cut to the computer itself.

The move confirms that the PC market has entered a more competitive phase. IBM remains the standard other makers invoke, but buyers now have enough alternatives to make price a weapon—and the summer of 1984 is opening with that weapon drawn.

stories.headline: Postal Service Votes to Abandon E-COM
body: The U.S. Postal Service’s governors voted June 6 to end E-COM, the hybrid electronic-mail service that accepted messages electronically and delivered printed copies through the mail. The retreat closes a costly government experiment after private carriers argued they could serve electronic messaging without postal competition.

E-COM never became the universal bridge its planners imagined. Its end leaves commercial data services, office networks and private electronic-message firms to define more of the emerging market—while ordinary home modem users continue discovering online communication one dial-up connection at a time.

stories.headline: Computer Games Start Learning New Tricks
body: June’s home-computer press asked whether games could begin to think for themselves. Designers were moving beyond fixed arcade patterns toward opponents and worlds that reacted to a player’s choices, a natural fit for disk-based machines with more memory than consoles.

The ambition is visible on store shelves: M.U.L.E. turns competition into a shifting economic contest, while Bruce Lee advertises twenty settings and two distinct adversaries. The attraction is no longer merely faster action but the feeling that the machine can surprise its owner.

stories.headline: Copy Protection Draws Fire from Paying Customers
body: A June COMPUTE!'s Gazette exchange put software piracy and copy protection on the same page. A retailer argued that high prices and restrictions on backup copies could alienate legitimate customers even as publishers tried to stop unauthorized duplication.

The magazine’s own Gazette Disk supplied a pointed contrast: the editor reported that it was selling well while remaining unprotected. The debate exposes a problem with no easy answer—protecting a program without making the honest buyer’s disk more fragile or less useful.

bbsNote.summary: The June Gazette devoted a standing Home Telecommunications column to getting Commodore owners online, while the Postal Service's E-COM retreat underscored the growing boundary between private online services and public hybrid electronic mail.

posts.text: Robert Sims's monthly column gave owners practical context for modem use and online communication.
The June 6 vote to end E-COM left private electronic-message firms with less government competition.

curiosity.headline: A magazine disk shipped without copy protection
curiosity.summary: At the height of the software-piracy debate, COMPUTE!'s Gazette made a conspicuous consumer-friendly choice.
curiosity.detail: The editor told readers the new Gazette Disk was doing well and was still unprotected, then printed a retailer's argument that copy protection alienated legitimate buyers who wanted backups.

undergroundDesk.headline: Copy-Protection Backlash Reaches the Letters Page
undergroundDesk.dek: Publishers confront piracy while customers demand usable backups.
body: A June Gazette exchange described unauthorized copying as a genuine threat to software makers, but it also recorded a growing backlash from paying customers. Retailers warned that restrictive protection and high prices could make the conflict worse.

No crew or bulletin board was named, and the dispute offered no simple cure. The magazine’s unprotected companion disk became a quiet test of whether convenience and fair pricing could earn customer loyalty.
